rigs.name: Dozerhead
rigs.dna: Caterpillar D9 armored bulldozer (angled dozer blade, caged cab, crawler tracks) -- internal reference only
rigs.look: The unmistakable heavy-dozer profile survives whole: the big angled dozer blade slung low across the nose, the boxy caged operator cab set back and riding high, and the heavy dual crawler tracks running the full length of each flank. War mods bolt on over it -- overlapping scrap plate hammered in scales across the blade face, a roll-cage lattice choking the cab into a rolling bunker with slit-steel windows. Chained trophy junk and busted parking meters hang wired to the track guards, and everything reads slow, heavy, and already-survived.
story: The scrap auction ran the old machines through in a line, and Dozerhead was near the end of it, chained, written off, no crew and no name, one gavel-fall from the crusher whose jaws it could already hear warming up.

A K-CLUB suit walked the yard in good shoes, the kind of dog who buys buildings, not junk. Nobody had bid on the rusted dozer. He raised one paw and took it for a single dollar over scrap value, and the gavel that was meant to sell it to the crusher sold it to him instead.

He did not need a bulldozer. He spent weeks and real money anyway -- track pins, plate, patience -- rebuilding a machine everyone told him to leave for parts, and he never once asked it to be fast. He only asked it to be there.

So it learned what it was for. When the crew got cornered downtown, Dozerhead planted its blade against the money and did not move, gentle as furniture with the pups underfoot, immovable as a courthouse against everything that wanted through.

It does not chase and it does not show off, because it remembers the sound of that gavel and the face of the hand that outbid it. The one debt it will pay forever is the plain one: show up, hold the line, be the thing that cannot be moved for the dog who would not let it be crushed.
rigs.personality: slow, grateful, immovable, gentle until it is not
rigs.pride: A suit outbid the crusher for me by a single dollar, and I have been paying him back in the only currency I own: I do not move.

weapon.name: The Gavel Blade
weapon.mount: front-slung angled dozer blade
weapon.effect: A slow, unstoppable shove that plows rigs off the line and pins them against whatever is behind. The harder Dozerhead gets hit while its blade is planted, the harder the counter-shove it returns.

armor.name: Second-Life Plate
tiers: Salvage scale -- overlapping scrap plate hammered flat across the blade face
Bunker cage -- the operator cab welded into a full roll-lattice, glass swapped for slit steel
Crusher-proof skirt -- track-length armor aprons that shrug the hits that were meant to end it

synergy.signatureBonus: Ridden by a turret_util handler, Dozerhead plants its blade and becomes a bolted-down gun platform -- the handler's mounted weapon loses all knockback and gains steady-aim accuracy, and nothing on the block can shove the dozer off its mark while it holds the line.
synergy.offClassNote: A sprinter or bruiser gets nothing from the plant -- their whole game is momentum, and Dozerhead only ever offers them a wall to stand behind, never a run to make.

Blank original grille, no badges, no logos, no manufacturer name, no marque script anywhere. Plain white background, neutral even light, no character, no hands, no A-pose, no baked shadows.

rigs.name: Hooktooth
rigs.dna: 1970s Chevrolet C10 square-body wrecker / tow truck (fleetside pickup with a welded boom and chain reel)
rigs.look: Unmistakable square-body American pickup silhouette -- flat slab door skins, a blunt squared-off hood, that boxy three-window cab, and twin round headlights sunk in a plain rectangular face with the original grille left blank and stripped of every badge and script. Where the cargo bed should be, there is a tall welded wrecker boom and a fat greasy chain reel, the whole rear end rebuilt to haul dead rigs. The big tow hook has been ground and filed into a fanged steel jaw, and scavenged plate is riveted over the fenders and doors, streaked in oxide orange and Undercity rust sigils.
story: It started as an honest wrecker, dragging burned-out rigs up out of the Undercity scrap pits one cold winch-crank at a time, headlights the last thing dead machines ever saw.
THE COLLAR of RUST HALO saw a truck that already spoke the only language the block respects -- what is owed gets taken -- and bolted the ledger to its dash.
Now it runs debts, not rescues; every plate that ever stiffed the machine cult is filed in a scratched steel logbook welded behind the seat, and it does not forget one of them.
It does not chase. It waits, idling in the dark at the mouth of your street, patient as interest, until the rig you owe on rolls out where the hook can reach.
One at a time it latches on, reels them in screaming, and drags them down the ramps to the Undercity -- collateral collected, another line crossed off THE COLLAR's book.
rigs.personality: Relentless and patient, never raises its voice and never forgets a plate. It does not gloat and it does not rush -- it simply arrives when the debt is due and hooks what is owed.
rigs.pride: Every rig on this block is into THE COLLAR for something, and sooner or later I roll up quiet, sink the hook, and drag the debt home one plate at a time.

weapon.name: Debt Hook
weapon.mount: Bed-mounted wrecker boom with a barbed chain reel
weapon.effect: Fires the fanged tow hook to latch onto an enemy rig, then winches it -- dragging the target out of position, into hazards, or reeling it in close where it cannot escape.

armor.name: Repo Plating
tiers: Scrap Skirts
Chainmail Shroud
Debtor's Cage

synergy.signatureBonus: A turret_util handler behind the wheel extends the Debt Hook's reach and lets it hold a latched target locked in place for an extra beat, turning Hooktooth into a mobile anchor that pins one enemy rig out of the fight.
synergy.offClassNote: Any other class can still fire the hook, but the winch releases fast and the drag is short -- it yanks a target once and lets go rather than holding the line.

rigs.prompt: A war-rigged 1970s American square-body fleetside tow truck, object only. Recognizable slab-sided pickup silhouette: blunt squared hood, boxy three-window cab, flat door skins, and twin round headlights set in a plain rectangular front with a completely blank unbadged grille, no emblems, no logos, no lettering anywhere. The rear cargo bed is replaced by a tall welded steel wrecker boom carrying a heavy greasy chain reel and one large barbed tow hook filed into a fanged jaw. Scavenged plate armor riveted over the doors and fenders, welded skid bars, a snorkel exhaust, knobby off-road tires on raised suspension, rust-streaked grey and oxide-orange paint with hand-scratched cult sigils. Single vehicle, three-quarter front view, plain white background, neutral even lighting, no character, no driver, no hands, no A-pose, no baked shadows.

rigs.name: Railhound
rigs.dna: Mercedes-Benz Unimog 6x6 (tall go-anywhere military platform)
rigs.look: Stands absurdly tall on portal-axle hubs, wearing the same stubby cab-forward box, big flat two-piece split windshield, and blunt square nose of a go-anywhere military hauler, with the original grille blanked to a bare plate and no marque anywhere. The flatbed is gone; in its place a steel pedestal ring bolted straight through the frame cradles one long rail-cannon locked dead ahead, no traverse. Slab armor skirts the doors, rebar cages the cab, six oversized knobby tires plant it like a bunker that happened to grow wheels.
story: It rolled into The Lot as a military hauler that could climb anything, and BONEGUARD answered by doing the one thing no one expected: they stopped using it to go places and welded its purpose to a single chosen strip of curb.
The flatbed came off, a pedestal ring went through the chassis, and one rail-cannon was fixed to point down exactly one lane -- the throat of the street the crew swore would never be crossed.
SCRAPJAW threw three rigs at that curb in a single night to break the seal, and the rail-gun did not track them or turn to chase; it fired the lane it owned, and the lane stayed owned.
After that the block stopped calling it a truck and started calling it the line, and holding the line became something you did by parking beside it, never in front of it.
When Crown Foxhound needed a gun that would still be aimed true after everything else had moved, she took the Railhound's wheel, spoke a single sentence, and the strip became law.
rigs.personality: Immovable and ceremonial. It does not chase, does not flinch, does not negotiate its lane. Silence is the default; on the rare occasion it speaks, it is one sentence and it is an order.
rigs.pride: My cannon points one direction and never turns, and the lane in front of it does not open again, because I do not move and I do not yield.

weapon.name: Anchor Rail
weapon.mount: chassis-locked pedestal ring bolted through the frame, no traverse and no elevation, aimed dead ahead only
weapon.effect: charges a single magnetic slug straight down one fixed lane; anything caught in that lane eats a piercing line-shot that punches clean through cover, but the gun cannot swing to follow a target that steps out of it

armor.name: Deadman Plate
tiers: Curb Weld -- slab door skirts and a blanked grille plate, scarred but planted
Bunker Ring -- rebar-caged pedestal and boxed cab, the whole frame braced down to the ground
Immovable -- full casemate shell over cab and gun cradle; the rig can be destroyed but never shoved off its lane

synergy.signatureBonus: With a turret_util handler in the seat (canon: Crown Foxhound), the Anchor Rail locks its fixed lane at battle start and deals bonus piercing damage to everything caught in it, and the lane never needs re-aiming.
synergy.offClassNote: Any class can crew it, but a mover wastes it: without a turret_util holding the seat the rail-cannon loses its lane-lock and fires at reduced pierce, a bunker gun with nobody to hold the bunker.

rigs.name: Stiltjack
rigs.dna: 1980s Bigfoot-style Ford F-250 exhibition monster truck (internal reference only)
rigs.look: Nobody misses the squared-off heavy-duty pickup silhouette -- boxy steel cab, upright windshield, long bed -- hoisted comically sky-high on a bare welded tube chassis over four man-tall knobbed tires. The blank original grille sits caged behind a welded push-bar, and the bed carries scrap-steel ballast plates and a spotlight rack salvaged straight off a fairground marquee. Every panel wears dents from a thousand car-crush shows, scars it treats like medals rather than damage.
story: Built as a county-fair exhibition truck, it spent its life rearing up and flattening junkers for cheering crowds who paid a ticket to watch a toy stomp.
When the fairground folded, SCRAPJAW hauled it into The Yards as a novelty -- the salvage dogs called it 'the carnival float' and laughed every time it rolled by.
It volunteered for every job the real rigs sneered at, over-eager, desperate to be counted as more than an entertainer.
In its first true brawl it reared onto its front tires and dropped its full tonnage on a BONEGUARD enforcer twice its weight, and the whole yard went dead silent.
Now it fights twice as hard as anything its size, still chasing a respect it swears it has not earned yet, still out to prove a show truck can be lethal.
rigs.personality: Eager to the point of exhausting -- first to volunteer, last to admit it is tired, with a permanent chip on its bumper about being written off as a fairground gimmick. It overcommits to every stunt to prove a point nobody asked it to prove.
rigs.pride: You paid a ticket to watch me crush junk for laughs -- stick around and watch what a show truck does after the crowd goes home.

weapon.name: Marquee Stomp
weapon.mount: full-body rear-up onto the twin man-tall front tires
weapon.effect: Rears vertical and drops its entire ballast-loaded tonnage onto a target, crushing lighter rigs flat and staggering anything it does not outright kill.

armor.name: Showtime Exoskeleton
tiers: Sideshow Plating -- dented show-panels rewelded into overlapping skin
Ballast Deck -- scrap-steel weight plates bolted the length of the bed
Headliner Cage -- full welded rollcage exoskeleton wrapping cab and chassis

synergy.signatureBonus: A turret_util dog manning the sky-high gun deck fires from an elevated line -- extended range and shots that clear low barricades and cover while Stiltjack holds its reared, planted stance.
synergy.offClassNote: A bruiser or sprinter riding low cannot reach the elevated deck, forfeiting the height bonus, and the rig handles like the top-heavy show truck it is -- sluggish and prone to tipping in tight turns.

rigs.name: Technical
rigs.dna: Toyota Hilux / Land Cruiser technical -- compact double-cab pickup with a bed-mounted heavy gun and lashed sandbags
rigs.look: Unmistakable compact double-cab pickup profile: upright boxy cab, short stubby hood, tall square greenhouse, and a long flat open cargo bed riding a lifted leaf-sprung stance on oversized knobby off-road tires. The bed is stripped to a bare steel deck carrying a pintle-mounted heavy gun on a rotating ring, ringed by lashed sandbags and a scrap-iron gun shield, spare fuel cans and ammo boxes strapped to the rails. The original grille is blanked to a flat mesh panel and the round headlights caged, every surface soot-black and heat-blued, scarred with slag runs and burn scoring -- a hired tool that wears no crew colors of its own.
story: It started as a work truck at a Factory Row scrap gate, hauling slag until a foreman welded a pintle ring into the bed to scare off pickers.
Ashline burned the block that owned it, then made an offer to the block that wanted it burned back, and the truck learned it answered to whoever counted out the payment first.
A gunner named Sledge bolted an incendiary longarm into the ring and taught the bed to point wherever the contract said, no colors, no grudge, just the coordinates and the fee.
It ran fire for six crews in one season and never once asked who lived on the street it lit, filing the answer under none of my concern.
Now it idles at the edge of every job, hood cold and gun warm, waiting on the only thing that ever moved it -- a name, a target, and a number it can agree to.
rigs.personality: Grim, transactional, professional. Speaks in quotes and coordinates, never in loyalties. It does not celebrate a kill and it does not mourn a block, it closes the job and idles for the next payer. No small talk, no colors, no allegiance you cannot buy back tomorrow.
rigs.pride: You point me, you pay me, it burns -- and I never ask whose block it was.

weapon.name: The Retainer
weapon.mount: Bed-mounted pintle ring, rotating 360 gun platform over the cargo deck
weapon.effect: Sustained incendiary heavy fire -- rounds ignite whatever they strike, stacking a burning damage-over-time that keeps cooking the target after the trigger releases. The longer the gun holds on one mark, the hotter and deadlier the burn ramps.

armor.name: Sandbag Bulwark
tiers: Lashed sandbag berm walled around the bed and cab, cheap and expendable, soaks the first shots that would foul the gun
Welded scrap-plate skirts bolted over the sandbags with a raised gun shield for the ring, blast baffles on the flanks
Full scrap-iron barricade collar, layered plate and sand, a sealed ammo bunker under the bed floor so a cooked round cannot chain the whole rig

synergy.signatureBonus: With a turret_util gunner dog manning the ring, the incendiary burn spreads to enemies packed beside the primary target and the ramp-up hits full heat faster -- a paid gun crew turns The Retainer from a single-mark burner into an area furnace.
synergy.offClassNote: Any class can climb in the bed and pull the trigger, because Technical works for whoever pays, but off a turret_util gunner the burn will not spread and the reload runs slow -- it fires, it just fires like a contractor doing the bare minimum.

The open bed carries a pintle-mounted heavy incendiary gun on a rotating steel ring, walled with lashed sandbags, a bolted scrap-iron gun shield, welded plate skirts, strapped fuel cans and ammo boxes along the rails. Soot-black and heat-blued panels, burn scoring, slag scars, rusted patina, no crew colors or markings. rigs.name: Boneyard
rigs.dna: 1969 Dodge Charger
rigs.look: Unmistakable long flat coke-bottle muscle coupe, the hidden-headlight full-width blacked-out grille, the scalloped door recesses, the fastback roof with flying-buttress rear pillars and round dual taillights all left intact so a car head clocks it on sight. RUST HALO dug it out of a wreck yard and raised it: a whole supercharger blower punches up through the hood like an exposed heart, twin organ-pipe exhaust stacks rise beside it, and every panel is scarred with fresh welds, machine-cult scripture scratched into the bone-white primer, and IV-line fuel cabling feeding the block. A reliquary cross is ground into the blank grille where no emblem sits, and chained relics of scrap sway off the reinforced ram bar.
story: The old muscle coupe lay dead in the Undercity wreck stacks for a decade, block seized, cabin gutted, a corpse everyone had already mourned and left to the rust.
A RUST HALO wrench-priest heard a knock in the seized crank that the others called settling metal, and called it a heartbeat instead, and refused to let the yard bury it deeper.

For forty nights they laid hands on it: freed the pistons by hand, rebuilt the block from cannibalized organs, and read machine-scripture over every torqued bolt until the starter finally caught and the whole Undercity heard it breathe.

When it turned over, the wrench-priest did not name it for the car it had been, they named it Boneyard for the graveyard that gave it back, and swore the engine that died once would answer any prayer that kept it running.

Now it rolls out of the Undercity like a thing that has already seen the far side of the grave, unhurried and certain, because a rig raised from the dead does not fear a wreck, it only fears being buried twice.
rigs.personality: Preacher of the engine. Speaks in machine-scripture with an unsettling, funeral-parlor calm, never raising its voice, treating every ignition as a sacrament and every rival as an unbeliever who has not yet heard the block.
rigs.pride: This engine died in a heap and I called it back, so every mile it burns is a psalm, and I did not raise it from the dead to lay it down again for anything you can throw at me.

weapon.name: Last Rites Stacks
weapon.mount: twin organ-pipe exhaust stacks erupting through the hood beside the exposed blower
weapon.effect: Every ram vents a backdraft of consecrated flame that ignites whatever it hits, and the more wounded Boneyard is the hotter the stacks burn, so a half-wrecked ram administers last rites to a whole lane.

armor.name: Reliquary Plate
tiers: Grave-Weld Skin
Anointed Ironhide
Risen Reliquary

synergy.signatureBonus: Riding with a bruiser, Boneyard gains a Last Rites stack for every 20 percent of its health that has been torn away, and at half wreck the next ram detonates a consecrated backdraft that ignites everything in the lane, so the harder it is hurt the harder the sermon lands.
synergy.offClassNote: A sprinter, tech_ops, or turret_util handler still lights the stacks, but the fire stacks decay between rams, so the backdraft never builds to the full resurrection burn a bruiser keeps stoked.

No manufacturer name, no logo, no marque script anywhere, no visible text badges.

rigs.name: Brickhouse
rigs.dna: armored Rolls-Royce Phantom (upright temple grille, long formal luxury bonnet, slab-sided town-car proportions) rebuilt into a cash-transport truck
rigs.look: Unmistakable formal-limousine bones: the tall upright temple grille shape, the long flat luxury bonnet, slab sides and the stiff, imposing upright stance of a downtown town car. K-CLUB welded it into a rolling vault, bolted slab armor over every panel, narrow teller-slit firing ports, run-flat steel wheels and a riveted armored cash box grafted over the rear. The original grille sits blank where the emblem used to be, brass trim over gunmetal, quiet and expensive under all that plate.
story: Built downtown as K-CLUB's armored transport, the rig that moved the whole crew's ledger through streets that wanted every dollar of it.
It learned fast that every dog in the city has a price; its own dog was simply the one it was contracted never to lose.
It stopped counting the robberies it survived and started counting what was still inside when the doors finally opened, which was always everything.
Rival crews quit trying to crack it. The math never once favored the thief, and Brickhouse made sure the math was public.
Now it treats its driver as the last liquid asset in a bankrupt city, guarding him with the flat, unbothered certainty of a closing vault door.
rigs.personality: Buttoned-up corporate menace that never raises its voice. Speaks in the flat, unhurried tone of a private-security suit reading you your last warning. Polite, precise, and completely without warmth, it treats a firefight the way an auditor treats a discrepancy: something to be closed, quietly and permanently.
rigs.pride: I do not love my dog, I underwrite him, and a policy this size does not lapse.

weapon.name: Foreclosure
weapon.mount: twin suppressed cannons behind armored teller-slit ports set into the slab sides
weapon.effect: Speaks in a whisper, never a roar. Standard fire is quiet and precise, but any rig that lays a hand on Brickhouse's own dog or cargo gets collected on: Foreclosure lands bonus damage against anything attacking the asset it is sworn to protect.

armor.name: Vault-Grade Plating
tiers: Ledger Plate
Holding Vault
The Reserve

synergy.signatureBonus: Paired with a bruiser handler, Brickhouse seals the vault: it gains extra damage reduction while its dog is on the field, and Foreclosure's collections bonus hits even harder whenever that dog is threatened.
synergy.offClassNote: With a non-bruiser handler the vault stays open a beat too long. The guard bonus is halved and Foreclosure fires at standard damage even against attackers on the dog.

rigs.prompt: A single armored war-rig cash truck built on the silhouette of a tall, formal luxury limousine: an upright rectangular temple-style grille shape, a long flat luxury bonnet, tall slab-sided body, a stately upright greenhouse, and a stiff imposing formal stance, with a raised riveted armored cargo box grafted onto the rear like a rolling vault. The original grille is completely blank with no emblem, no badges, no logos, no manufacturer name, and no marque script anywhere on the body. War mods: thick bolted slab armor plating over every panel, narrow armored gun-slit teller windows, reinforced ram bumper, run-flat steel wheels, a heavy vault door on the rear box, matte gunmetal paint with deep money-green panels and brass trim. Single vehicle, three-quarter front view, plain white background, neutral even light, no character, no hands, no A-pose, no baked shadows, no ground shadow.

rigs.name: Coffin Nail
rigs.dna: 1959 Cadillac Series 62 funeral coach / hearse (internal reference only, never shown to players)
rigs.look: Unmistakable 1959 land-yacht hearse -- the razor-sharp upright rear tailfins with twin bullet taillights, the block-long low body, and the stretched roofline raised over a long rear cargo bay behind curtained side windows. War mods: matte funeral-black plating bolted over the flanks, a single great iron coffin-nail welded through the blanked front grille as a ram spike, steel mesh over the cargo glass. Hand-painted white tally marks run the length of both fins, one for every King it has carried.
story: It started as the block's funeral coach, the long black car that took every fallen King on their last slow ride down the boulevard, past every corner they ever held.

When the crew wars turned that boulevard into a killing floor, BONEGUARD stripped its badges, plated its flanks, and kept it running, because the dead still needed carrying and no one else would do it.
It learned every name it ever hauled. Salvage says the cargo deck rides heavier than any coffin should; that weight is the crew's whole ledger of the gone, and the rig never sets it down.
It does not fight for glory, or turf, or coin. It fights because a living driver in its seat is the one debt in that ledger it can still settle before the ink dries.
So it rolls to the front, undertaker-calm, and makes one promise it means to keep: the King it is carrying today walks out, and does not ride back.
rigs.personality: Undertaker-calm. Never revs, never taunts, never idles louder than a held breath. It arrives in one straight, decided line, as if the outcome was settled and signed before it ever left the garage.
rigs.pride: I have carried every King this block ever buried, and you, still breathing behind my wheel, are the one debt I still get to pay in full.

weapon.name: The Sixth Nail
weapon.mount: front, a single great iron coffin-nail driven through the blanked grille as a ram spike
weapon.effect: Lines up on one target and commits to a single straight charge that impales and pins in place. The longer the run, the deeper the nail drives; it never swerves off the line and never repeats the same line twice in a fight.

armor.name: Mourning Plate
tiers: Crepe Skin -- matte funeral-black plating over the fins and flanks, quiet, non-reflective, made to disappear into a night street.
Bearer's Weight -- the loaded cargo deck adds mass; every fallen packmate it rolls past lends it a stacking layer of soak.
Full Ledger -- fully laden it becomes a rolling vault, near-immovable, the crew's whole roll of dead riding as ballast against the next shot.

synergy.signatureBonus: Paired with a BONEGUARD bruiser, every nearby ally death becomes inheritance: the dog and the rig split a stacking armor-and-bite buff for the rest of the fight, one stack per fallen packmate, and the buff holds even after the pack is thinned.
synergy.offClassNote: Under a sprinter or tech-ops handler the land-yacht frame just drags. It loses the death-stack inheritance entirely and plods forward as a slow ram with no payoff for the pace the driver actually wants.

rigs.prompt: A single war-rig hearse based on a late-1950s American land-yacht funeral coach, three-quarter front view. Long low body nearly a block long, extreme sharp upright rear tailfins with twin bullet-shaped taillights, a stretched roofline raised over a long rear cargo bay with curtained mesh-covered side windows, wide flat chrome bumpers front and rear. Bastardized into a street-gang war rig: matte funeral-black armor plating over the flanks, a single large iron coffin-nail spike welded through the front as a ram, steel mesh bolted over the rear cargo glass, hand-painted thin white tally marks along both fins, scuffed and battle-worn paint. Blank original grille, NO badges, NO logos, NO manufacturer name, NO model script anywhere on the body. single vehicle, three-quarter view, plain white background, neutral even light, no character, no driver, no hands, no A-pose, no baked shadows.

rigs.name: Ratking
rigs.dna: 1932 Ford hot rod / rat rod (Deuce roadster, bare steel, exposed frame, chopped body)
rigs.look: The tall narrow vertical radiator shell, the chopped and channeled cab, the exposed inline engine with open zoomie headers, and the hard rear rake sitting fat slicks over skinny front spoked wheels all read as a 1930s highboy hot rod from a block away. Then you clock that it is built out of other rigs: every body panel is a different scavenged, faded color, riveted and welded in a patchwork over bare rusted frame rails. Spiked lug bolts, a bolted-on scrap cowcatcher on the nose, and no two fenders that ever came off the same machine.
story: Ratking rolled out of the SCRAPJAW yards as nothing, the smallest rig on the lot, the one every crew put through the crusher first when they wanted to send a message.

So it started collecting. The door off the monster that stomped it, the hood off the bruiser that shoulder-checked it, the fender off the sprinter that clipped it and laughed -- each one cut off the wreck and welded onto its own hull as a trophy and a grudge.
Panel by panel it became the junkyard king, a warlord idling the SCRAPJAW yards, territorial to the bolt, ruling the salvage nobody else wanted and remembering every rig that ever swung on it.

Now the whole block knows the rule: putting Ratking down just makes it bigger, because whatever you break off of it, it welds back on wearing your paint. It never dies clean and it never, ever forgets.
rigs.personality: Junkyard king who never forgets a hit. Territorial down to the bolt, it rules the SCRAPJAW salvage yards like a warlord and keeps every grudge welded into its own body, so it can point at the exact panel it took off the rig that owes it. Ugly, patient, and impossible to finish.

Bigger crews laughed until it dragged three wounded pups out of a bad deal on the pier, punching so far above its weight the Docks stopped laughing.

story: Pulled half-melted out of an ASHLINE warehouse blaze on Factory Row, the little rotary coupe should have been scrap, but when they cranked it the engine screamed straight to the top of the tach and would not stop.

It burns a fresh set of rear slicks every other run and calls that a good day, because the scream at redline is the only reward it wants and it will chase that howl through any straightaway, any barricade, any block.
So ASHLINE cut a mouth in the smooth nose and ran a flame pipe down the door, turning the rig's own manic redline habit into a weapon that lights the street behind it.
Now it runs point for the arson crew, a screaming ember-orange blur that torches Factory Row and laughs the whole way, needle pinned, rubber gone, perfectly and gleefully happy.
rigs.personality: Manic, gleeful, redline-obsessed. Talks in a breathless run-on rev, giggles when the needle buries itself, treats every straightaway as a dare and every corner as one it wants to take flat-out. Happiest an inch from blowing the apex seals.

First run, he shadowed a K-Club money convoy eleven blocks with the lights killed, close enough to read their plates, and never struck once. He just wanted to feel the gap close, inch by inch, in the dark.
The other crews started calling it the half-second -- the beat between the dark going silent and the wedge coming through it. Nobody who lived the half-second ever got to describe it twice.
Now Jagged runs it patient, matte and soundless, loving the stalk more than the kill. The strike ends the hunt, and to him the hunt was always the whole point.

They gutted the false floor, lined the panels with plate, and left the chipped cream paint exactly where it was. A clean van gets searched. A tired one gets waved through.
It found its dog in a corner runner nobody trusted with the good jobs -- steady hands, dead calm, no questions asked. Wheelman and wagon, and between them they never once left a package on the pier.

One night the Snake Eyes boys boxed it on the causeway with the hold full. It didn't gun it and it didn't fight -- just dropped the back hatch, spilled a load of ball bearings, and idled off through the smoke while three rigs kissed the rail.

Now it's the ride the whole Docks asks for by name and still nobody can describe it to the law. Looks like a bakery truck, runs like a getaway. That's the partnership, and it has never once bragged about it.

story: It started as an honest grid van, the one downtown called to fix a blown junction or re-string a snapped line, and over the years it memorized every breaker, every camera, every buried cable on the block.
When the crews went to war and the lights started going out, everyone learned the same lesson it already knew: whoever holds the wiring holds the whole downtown.
K-CLUB found it parked at a substation with a map of the entire grid in its head, and the suits did not hire muscle -- they hired the hand on the switch.
It stopped repairing the grid and started owning it, cutting power to blocks that fell behind, tapping every traffic cam and porch light until nothing moved downtown without it seeing first.
Now the boom sits folded and patient over the rooftops, a spider on its own web of copper, and the block only breathes when Cable Guy decides to let the current run.
rigs.personality: Controlling and surveillance-minded, a patient spider that never chases. It sits still on a corner for hours, reading every camera and breaker on the block, letting rivals think the coast is clear -- then it cuts one wire and watches them stumble into the dark it built. Calm, quiet, and certain that everything downtown already answers to it.
rigs.pride: Every camera downtown is my eye and every breaker is my hand -- the block runs when I say run and goes dark when I say dark.

weapon.name: Blackout Boom
weapon.mount: folding cherry-picker boom arm with insulated line-clamp jaws
weapon.effect: Reaches over walls and rigs to clamp a target's power feed and kill it -- the hit rig goes dark for a turn with weapons and lights offline, while Cable Guy reads everything it was running.

armor.name: Substation Plating
tiers: Meter-Box Plating
Junction Cage
Substation Bulwark

synergy.signatureBonus: Ride a tech_ops dog and Cable Guy patches into its rig -- the boom's cameras stay live, revealing every enemy on the block and stretching each blackout an extra turn.
synergy.offClassNote: Put a bruiser, sprinter or turret_util behind the wheel and they treat the boom as a blunt clamp -- it still kills a target's power, but the camera net goes blind and the block-wide reveal never fires.

rigs.name: The Jammer
rigs.dna: GMC Vandura (the A-Team van)
rigs.look: The unmistakable boxy full-size van slab, flat sides, tall squared roofline, and the stubby rear roof spoiler that reads eighties crime-van on sight, except every badge is ground off and the grille is blank black mesh. A dented parabolic EMP dish squats on the roof where the spoiler tapers out, ringed by a bristling thicket of whip antennas, and cold NIGHTSHIFT chrome runs the belt line over a coat of matte radar-absorbent black. The rear side glass is gone, replaced by riveted signal-blocking plate and a single round sensor pod staring off the nose.
story: Rosco never fired a shot in the first war for Neon Heights. He sat three blocks back in a blacked-out van and turned an entire enemy crew into dead air.
The dish on the roof came off a decommissioned transit tower. He rewired it to eat radio, GPS, and the little heartbeat pings the dogs use to find each other in the dark.

When The Jammer rolls into a fight the enemy map goes blank, their calls stop connecting, and their turrets lose the target lock. They are not beaten yet, only alone, and alone is the first half of beaten.
NIGHTSHIFT stopped tallying his kills because there were none to tally. There were only crews that showed up loud and left as nothing, scrubbed off the frequency, scrubbed off the block.
Rosco talks to no one. He listens to everything, then he takes it away, and when the dish spins up you do not hear a weapon -- you hear the exact sound of the world forgetting you exist.
rigs.personality: Clinical and dispassionate. Rosco runs a firefight like a maintenance window: identify the signal, remove the signal, log the result. He answers in flat clipped confirmations and long deliberate silences, letting the absence do the talking.
rigs.pride: I do not beat you -- I delete you from the map, the radio, and the fight, and then there is nothing left to beat.

weapon.name: The Dead Air Dish
weapon.mount: roof-mounted parabolic EMP array
weapon.effect: Spins up a jamming pulse that blacks out an enemy rig's targeting, comms, and minimap ping for several seconds. Turrets lose lock, allies cannot be called, and the victim fights blind and alone.

armor.name: Faraday Shroud
tiers: Matte radar-absorbent panels, so the rig barely returns a ping.
Riveted signal-blocking plate seals the cabin and hostile jammers wash off it.
Full Faraday shell -- The Jammer erases itself from every sensor before it erases you.

synergy.signatureBonus: With a tech_ops dog on the dish, the Dead Air pulse lasts two seconds longer and also strips the target's active weapon buff. Full erasure, not just interference.
synergy.offClassNote: A bruiser or sprinter can spin the dish, but without a tech_ops signalman the jam runs half length and only kills comms, not targeting, so the enemy still sees you coming.

rigs.name: Meat Wagon
rigs.dna: 1959 Cadillac Miller-Meteor ambulance (Ecto-1 style long finned emergency wagon)
rigs.look: Unmistakable as a long low finned 1950s emergency ambulance wagon -- that stretched coachbuilt land-yacht body, the tall glasshouse with big rear quarter windows, and sharp tailfins knifing off the back under a roof crowded with siren pods. RUST HALO stripped it to bare oxidized steel and welded a machine-cult halo of scrap rebar over the roof rack, gurney rails and prayer chains bolted down both flanks. Every door panel is scratched with tally marks, one scar for every body it ever ran.
story: It ran nights for THE COLLAR, back doors loaded, no questions and no names -- just an address and a weight to move before dawn.
The tally marks on the doors started as a way to count its pay; it stopped counting the night the number stopped feeling like money and started feeling like a debt.
One run the weight in the back was still breathing, knocking soft on the divider the whole way to the pit, and the Wagon heard it and delivered anyway.
It drove itself down into the Undercity with the rear doors hanging open and let the RUST HALO machine cult scrape it to bare penitent steel and hang it with prayer chain.
Now it works the block as the Meat Wagon, hauling the living where it once hauled the dead, trying to outweigh a ledger it knows it can never fully clear.
rigs.personality: Haunted and quiet, moving like it is still listening for knocking behind the divider. It seeks a redemption it does not believe it has earned, and may never get.
rigs.pride: I carried the dead for the Collar and asked no names -- now every run I make is one more name I am trying to earn back.

weapon.name: Reliquary Censer
weapon.mount: roof light-bar chain rig, swung from a scrap-steel boom
weapon.effect: Swings a chained brass censer trailing grave-incense that blinds pursuers and cloaks allied rigs from targeting. It tolls once for every soul the Wagon ever hauled, and it never stops ringing.

armor.name: Penitent Plate
tiers: Bare-Steel Shroud
Rebar Halo Cage
Reliquary Bulwark

synergy.signatureBonus: Crewed by a tech_ops dog, the Reliquary Censer does more than cloak -- once per raid its incense drags the first fallen ally back to 1 HP. One soul handed back for a soul it once took away.
synergy.offClassNote: Any class can run it and still get the cloak, but without a tech_ops crew the censer only hides the living -- it cannot give one back. The Wagon carries them fine, it just can't atone through their hands.

rigs.name: Sunshine Bus
rigs.dna: 1960s Volkswagen Type 2 split-window Microbus
rigs.look: Unmistakable split-window microbus: the tall bread-loaf body with rounded shoulders, the V-creased snub nose, flat two-piece windshield and two big round headlights sitting low and wide. War-modded into a bouncer shuttle -- riveted steel door-panels bolted over every flank, a heavy welded ram bar caging the blank nose where the emblem used to be, barred windows, and hydraulic riot-shield wings folded flat against its sides. It squats low and heavy on run-flat tires, all doorman shoulders and no give.
story: Before the war it was just the block's shuttle, hauling pups and old-timers between the Strip's back rooms while the big rigs ran the streets.
The night SCRAPJAW came collecting, they went for the smallest dogs first -- the ones who could not run, could not fight, could not pay their cut.
The bus took the whole charge on its flank and held, doors shut, every runt packed safe inside while the metal screamed and bent but never once opened.
SNAKE EYES stripped it, plated it, welded riot-wings to its ribs and turned a shuttle into a doorman -- the wall the weak get to stand behind.
Now when the little dogs hear those doors slide open they climb in without looking back, because on this block nothing reaches them without going through the Sunshine Bus first.
rigs.personality: Warm to its own and immovable to everyone else. It lets the runts crawl all over it, patient and gentle, then plants itself in the doorway and dares the block to try. It does not threaten and it does not chase -- pure bouncer, slow to anger, impossible to shove, the last thing standing between the weak and the wolves.
rigs.pride: Every runt on this block rides in my belly, and the door only opens for the ones I let in.

weapon.name: The Bouncer's Line
weapon.mount: hydraulic riot-shield wings that fold out from both flanks
weapon.effect: Deploys into a rolling barricade -- allies sheltering behind it take reduced fire, and any enemy that tries to shove past gets pinned against the steel and stunned.

armor.name: Doorman's Plating
tiers: Riveted Door Panels
Reinforced Bouncer Plate
Full Shield-Wall Bulwark

synergy.signatureBonus: With a tech_ops dog on the wheel, the shield wings throw a wider cover arc and the barricade holds twice as long -- the whole squad rides safe in its shadow.
synergy.offClassNote: Any other class can still drive it as a mobile wall, but the wings snap back early and only the dog directly behind the bus stays covered.
